article_content: In the not-so-distant past, you could visit your local record shop and buy 'little disks of plastic' with the latest sounds from your favorite artists using your paper-route money. Chris Pirillo, president of Lockergnome.com, a blogging network, reminisces about the tangible music ownership experience. You could play them repeatedly until they were scratched beyond repair, lend them to friends, or even sell them to used record stores. The recording industry executives grew nervous as consumers made mix tapes, copying songs from purchased disks. As the digital age arrived, these executives began to loudly protest, leading to the development of Digital Rights Management (DRM). DRM effectively turned music consumption into a rental service, restricting how consumers could use purchased content. The author criticizes DRM for being consumer-unfriendly and likens it to being treated like a 'sharecropper' or 'serf'. Many feel that DRM is unfair and attempt to circumvent it, potentially leading to malware and other issues. The author notes that despite piracy concerns, 2007 was a record box office year, questioning who is truly being 'plundered'. Blogger Cory Doctorow is cited as finding DRM to be one of the most offensive digital constructs. The author prefers subscription services like Rhapsody and XM satellite radio but criticizes DRM for restricting content use. The article concludes that DRM is 'no good' and 'downright evil', advocating for its removal or significant change.

Chris Pirillo, Lockergnome.com ruvicha, he'i hese oñemomorãha umi ára oñemono'õ haguépe purahéi. Nde ikatúma ehechauka jeýpe ha jeýpe pe disco, emprésta nde irũnguérape, térã emoĩ nde archivo ryepýpe. Umi purahéi rehechaukáva ombyasy ojehai jey haguére disco-gui. article_content: You've probably sung along to Abba's 'Dancing Queen' a million times. But can you recite the lyrics right now? A nationwide poll found that the 1976 classic has the most commonly misheard song lyrics. Nearly a quarter of those surveyed got the words wrong, believing the Swedish quartet is singing about a more violent scenario. The correct lyric is 'See that girl, watch that scene, diggin' the dancing queen', but many think it's 'See the girl, watch her scream, kicking the dancing queen'. Other songs with misheard lyrics include Queen's 'We Will Rock You' and the Monkees' 'I'm A Believer'. The poll of 2,000 adults also found that 28% of respondents struggle to understand Ozzy Osbourne's lyrics.

Ñe'ẽ oĩva'ekue hekopete ha'e 'See that girl, watch that scene, diggin' the dancing queen', hákatu heta tapicha oĩ oñembohováihape 'See the girl, watch her scream, kicking the dancing queen'. article_content: The Loew's Kings Theatre in Brooklyn, New York, is being restored after lying dormant for over 35 years. The theatre, which first opened in 1929 and closed in 1977, is undergoing a $93 million regeneration project. New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg announced that the project will create 50 permanent jobs and 500 construction jobs. The theatre will be restored to its original grandeur, with a huge staircase, rose-coloured marble, and wood-panelled walls. It is expected to open in early 2015 and host over 200 concerts and performances annually.

article_content: WASHINGTON (CNN) -- A bronze statue of Helen Keller was unveiled at the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday. Lawmakers praised her as a trailblazer and inspiration for those with disabilities. The statue depicts the moment when Anne Sullivan spelled 'W-A-T-E-R' into Keller's hand. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said, 'Some are still dismissed and cast aside for nothing more than being less than perfect.' Alabama Gov. Bob Riley noted, 'Five simple letters helped rescue 7-year-old Helen Keller from a world of darkness and silence.' The statue shows Keller standing at a water pump, recognizing the connection between the manual alphabet and water. Keller learned to speak, earned a degree from Radcliffe College, and championed causes like women's suffrage and workers' rights. The statue is the Capitol's first depicting a child.

article_content: The Obama administration's swift decision to swap Russian spies caught in the U.S. is a misstep on multiple fronts. President Barack Obama prioritizes U.S.-Russian relations. There's a fine line between fostering a beneficial relationship and being overly accommodating. Dealing with Russia respectfully but firmly yields the best results historically. Moscow typically only agrees to terms that serve its self-interest. The rapid release of Russian deep-cover intelligence officers will likely be perceived as a sign of weakness by Prime Minister Vladimir Putin. This move undermines the deterrent against espionage. It also demotivates law enforcement, such as the FBI agents who invested time in these cases.

article_content: An American veterinarian, Stacey Addison, whose round-the-world trip was ruined in September when she was arrested in East Timor for drug smuggling after sharing a taxi with a stranger, has been released from prison on Christmas day. She spent four months in Gleno Women's Prison. Although released, Addison remains in East Timor as the government has not returned her passport. Her mother, Bernadette Kero, has started a petition on Change.org to help secure her return to the United States. Addison had planned her solo trip for nearly two years, visiting places like Antarctica and parts of Europe before arriving in southeast Asia. Her arrest occurred when she shared a taxi with a stranger who was smuggling methamphetamine. Despite being cleared of wrongdoing, with negative urine tests and no criminal record, she was initially detained and later arrested again on October 28. She is currently staying with former East Timorese President Jose Ramos-Horta, but is eager to return home as soon as her passport is returned.

article_content: 'Developing an HIV vaccine is challenging,' stated Dr. John Mascola, director of the Vaccine Research Center at the U.S. National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. The 2009 Thailand trial was a significant milestone, demonstrating a 31.2% reduction in HIV infection risk using a combination vaccine. Researchers are now preparing for a trial in South Africa, adapting the vaccine to target the prevalent HIV subtype in the region. The discovery of 'broadly neutralizing antibodies' has opened new avenues for creating a more effective HIV vaccine.

article_content: Florida health officials have confirmed eight cases of dengue fever in residents with no history of recent international travel, indicating the likely source is local mosquitoes. The cases were reported in two southeastern Florida counties: Martin and Miami-Dade. Dengue fever, which is transmitted by mosquitoes, is rare in the US but common in regions like Asia, India, the Caribbean, and Latin America. It causes symptoms such as high fever, rash, and joint pain, and can be fatal in severe cases. Florida has previously dealt with dengue fever outbreaks, notably in Key West during 2009 and 2010.

Dengue ryasýi, oñembohasa mosquitokuéra rupive, sa'i ojehecha EEUU-pe, hákatu hetáma Asia, India, Caribe ha Latinoamérica-pe. article_content: Paris (CNN) -- France and Germany celebrated the 50th anniversary of the Elysée Treaty in Berlin. Even British Prime Minister David Cameron waited 24 hours before delivering his speech on Europe. In 2003, Jacques Chirac hosted Chancellor Gerhard Schröder and the Bundestag at Versailles for the 40th anniversary. This year, Berlin hosted with a packed Bundestag, having added 577 extra seats for the French National Assembly. German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President François Hollande gave a joint press conference, met with students, and had lunch. The Elysée Treaty is a unique model of reconciliation. France and Germany have joint cabinet meetings and political partnerships. They've transitioned from a history of conflict to a strong friendship. The treaty is crucial as France and Germany are the EU's driving force, accounting for 40% of the eurozone's GDP, 33% of the EU's population, and 31% of its budget. It takes time for French presidents and German chancellors to develop a working relationship. Currently, with Hollande and Merkel, progress is slow due to their differing views on financial solidarity and political integration. The EU's future depends on Franco-German unity.

article_content: By Deni Kirkova and Simon Tomlinson. The photographer and his girlfriend, who leads him around the world, first caught our attention almost a year ago. Russian couple Murad Osmann and Nataly Zakharova have taken their signature photos in many exotic locations. Murad, 28, documents their travels by taking photos from his point of view as Nataly, 27, leads him. He is now set to release a book. Nataly wears traditional dress at the Moscow Kremlin. At the Hotel Du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes, France, and the Blue Mosque in Istanbul, Turkey, the couple's adventures continue. Each image shows Murad's extended hand holding Nataly's. Murad, an executive producer for Hype Productions, started this project in Barcelona in 2011. They have visited Madrid, New York City, Miami, Monaco, and Istanbul. 'The first photo happened in Barcelona while we were on vacation,' Murad said. 'Nataly was annoyed that I was always taking pictures, so she grabbed my hand.' Murad graduated as a civil engineer from Imperial College London but later pursued photography. 'We travel mostly for three to four days due to my work,' he said. His photos were initially taken with an iPhone. The images were included in an Art Basel exhibition at the Versace Mansion in Miami. Murad posts his 'Follow Me' photographs on Instagram, which has over 580,000 followers. They are planning to publish a book in the autumn.

article_content: WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Sen. Arlen Specter woke up at 4 a.m. one day last week with a severe headache, a side effect of chemotherapy. Ninety minutes later, he was on the squash court, playing with a partner less than half his age. That's how Specter faces cancer and chemotherapy. Borrowing a phrase from Winston Churchill, he calls it the 'never-give-in' approach. As he battles a recurrence of Hodgkin's disease, Specter, 78, a Pennsylvania Republican, plays squash nearly every day. He refers to these games as 'deposits in the health bank.' He maintains his rigorous work schedule. 'Doc,' he told CNN's Dr. Sanjay Gupta, 'I don't have time to think about Hodgkin's.' Hodgkin's disease is a rare but curable form of lymphoma. The treatment feels like 'a war of the worlds raging inside your body.' Specter has been through several major health crises over the past 30 years, including misdiagnoses and serious conditions. At 48, he was misdiagnosed with Lou Gehrig's disease. In 1993, he was told he had a cancerous brain tumor, but it was benign. It returned three years later. In 1998, he had heart bypass surgery. In 2005, he was diagnosed with Hodgkin's disease, which he overcame, but it has now recurred. Specter's oncologist, Dr. John Glick, emphasizes that his physical conditioning and mental attitude make him a strong candidate for aggressive treatment. 'The same treatment we would give somebody half his age,' Glick said. Specter's cardiologist, Dr. Howard Weitz, believes his continued hard work may be beneficial. 'I think for the hard worker who ceases working, their stress level increases,' Weitz said. Specter continues his squash routine despite reduced stamina and advises others to 'get a second opinion.'

Oñorairõvo jevy Hodgkin mba'asy rehe, Specter, 78 ary, Pennsylvania pegua, oha'ã squash hapichakuéra ndive ha oñe'ẽ 'depositokuéra banco de salud-pe' ichupekuéra. Oipytyvõ hembiapo asyete. 'Doc,' he'i CNN Dr. Sanjay Gupta-pe, 'ndajavyai Hodgkin rehe.' Hodgkin mba'asy ha'e peteĩ mba'asyete ojehu pya'e va'ekue, hákatu oñembotykete voi. article_content: In the dying days of the Battle of Mogadishu two years ago, on the beachside base used by Ugandan African Union troops in their successful campaign to drive Al-Shabaab from the capital, I came across three new prisoners. Handcuffed, dirty, and dejected, the eldest was 17, the youngest 15. They claimed to be volunteers who had surrendered when they became separated from their unit and ran out of bullets. 'We were given a piece of fruit every day,' one of them said. I later interviewed several Al-Shabaab deserters in a government camp. Instead of hardened jihadists, I found spirited teenagers, mostly instantly likeable. Their average age was 15; one, Liban, was 9. Like many young Somalis, Liban was an orphan; Al-Shabaab was his surrogate family. 'I'm not scared!' he said. 'I'm ready to fight again -- for the government!' These boy soldiers had little interest in Islamist ideology; they joined Al-Shabaab to survive, seeking security, food, and water. Until the Mogadishu government addresses these basic needs, Al-Shabaab will likely continue to find support. Children are useful to Al-Shabaab due to their capability for violence and courage. Liban's moral compass was absent; no one had shown him right from wrong. Al-Shabaab's recruitment includes misleading young recruits with false promises, such as showing Bollywood DVDs as footage from Paradise. Somali-American youth have been recruited, with at least 20 vanishing from their homes since 2007 to join Al-Shabaab. The FBI describes the recruitment process in Minneapolis as 'a very lateral, peer-to-peer organization.' Some recruits were dissatisfied with their experience, missing everyday comforts like McDonald's. The article highlights the contradictions in the actions of Al-Shabaab militants, citing an instance where a gunman gave a Mars Bar to a scolding child.

article_content: A young married couple, both in the Army, are spending Christmas apart despite being on tour in Afghanistan simultaneously. Lance Corporal Alisha Henderson and her husband, Corporal Paul Henderson, who are army chefs, work with different units, meaning they never get a chance to meet. They arrived in Helmand Province in September for a six-month tour. The couple met six years ago during an army training course and married the following year while on holiday in Cyprus. L/Cpl Henderson said being apart at Christmas will be difficult but it will have to be 'just like any other working day'. She will also celebrate her 24th birthday on Christmas Eve without her husband. L/Cpl Henderson serves with the 1st Battalion, The Mercian Regiment, while her husband, Cpl Henderson, is part of The Duke of Lancaster's Regiment. They communicate twice a week. The pair, who live in Catterick, North Yorkshire, recently returned from a two-week rest and relaxation period. Cpl Henderson said the break was the first time they had seen each other in three months. Over Christmas, L/Cpl Henderson will be at 1 MERCIAN's forward operating base in Shawqat, while Cpl Henderson will be working about 30 miles away at Patrol Base Attal.

article_content: The special police units blamed for the deadly shootings in Kyiv in February are, in part, a 'direct result' of the country's Soviet past. Ukraine has several special police forces, including the Security Service and the Berkut riot police, both of which have been 'widely implicated' in the Kyiv shootings. Senior Fellow Igor Sutyagin at London's Royal United Services Institute says he is 'not entirely surprised' that such forces have been mentioned and that several Berkut officers have been arrested. But he says early indications that most of the shooters were from Berkut are 'probably not entirely accurate'. 'I have some doubts whether it was exclusively Berkut, and whether it was mainly Berkut, because the radio communications intercepts show that there were Security Services snipers participating in that,' he said. 'Well, they were not alone, so there were probably, there might be Berkut snipers as well.' Sutyagin says the Berkut forces were mainly on the streets while the security police were deployed to the upper floors of buildings around the main protest site in Maidan Square and along Instytutska Street. Most of those killed were reportedly hit with bullets fired from above. The Berkut force was created in 1988, just three years before the Soviet Union fell. Independent Ukraine kept the force ostensibly as riot police, but Sutyagin says it became something else, in part because it answered to senior Interior Ministry officials, rather than police commanders. 'They were somehow sort of Praetorian Guards [body guards] for Ministry of Interior and maybe even for politicians.' 'And they obeyed their orders,' he said. 'And so, it is not about, mainly not about Berkut itself.' 'It is about orders which were issued for them to obey.' He says it makes sense that the Berkut and other well-disciplined, top-level forces operated under orders from senior officials on that bloody February day, as the government has charged. But Sutyagin also says that after two months on the freezing cold streets of Kyiv, the police officers were 'openly hostile' toward the protesters, who also hated them. He says that contributed to the violence that killed more than 100 people, mostly protesters, and brought down a government. The interim Ukrainian government's report implicates ousted president Viktor Yanukovych, and says Russian security service agents helped him plan and carry out the assault in mid-February. Yanukovych rejects the allegations. The Russian government has denied any involvement in the violence and blamed the deaths on the protesters.

article_content: JUBA, SOUTH SUDAN - South Sudan's warring parties have signed a 'significant' peace deal on Sunday, which is seen as the latest attempt to end the country's five-year civil war, having 'reportedly' killed tens of thousands and displaced millions. President Salva Kiir and former Vice-President Riek Machar 'allegedly' signed the agreement, according to Sudan's state news agency, SUNA. As part of the deal, Kiir will 'supposedly' remain president, and Machar will return as First Vice President, one of five vice presidents, 'sources indicate'. An eight-month pre-transitional period will be led by Kiir, followed by a three-year transitional period. The government will comprise 20 ministers from Kiir's party, nine from Machar's, and six from other groups, 'as per the agreement'. This is the latest of several peace agreements and cease-fires since the war broke out in 2013, with some analysts suggesting it may succeed. The first peace agreement 'allegedly' fell apart in July 2016 when fighting erupted in Juba, and Machar 'reportedly' fled on foot. He has been under house arrest in South Africa since then. South Sudan's government insists this time will be different; Machar has 'apparently' learned from his experiences and promised to work with Kiir, according to government spokesman Michael Makuei. Upon his return, Machar's troops will undergo training in cantonment sites to unify with the government army. One expert calls the deal 'a high-risk model', while others see potential. 'This peace deal sets up the same scenario for the third time,' said Alan Boswell, a South Sudan conflict analyst, but some experts believe this time could be different. Multiple cease-fires have been signed but 'mostly' violated within hours. The international community's patience is waning, and the U.N. Security Council imposed an arms embargo last month. In July, South Sudan's parliament extended the government's mandate until 2021, sparking opposition outrage. Feelings remain mixed. 'Of course peace will come because we're tired of war,' said Juba resident Santino Deng. Some rights groups welcome the deal but caution it's just a first step. 'To prevent a return to war, power must not be concentrated in a few hands,' said Brian Adeba, Enough Project. Edmund Yakani called the deal positive but remains unconvinced. 'The challenge lies with the political leaders,' he said.

article_content: Authorities in Utah evacuated a passenger plane on Thursday morning after receiving a bomb threat, said a spokeswoman for the Salt Lake City International Airport. The SkyWest plane, carrying 46 passengers and three crew members, was en route to Salt Lake City from Helena, Montana, when the threat was 'called in'. The Transportation Security Administration acknowledged an anonymous call threatening SkyWest Airline Flight 4654. The plane landed safely; law enforcement swept the aircraft with negative findings. All passengers and luggage were screened and released; the plane was to be put back into service, according to the FBI's Salt Lake City office.
